title: Our Messy Cyborg Past and Future - Nautilus
gist: Cultural historian Mike Jay, author of 'Wireheads', traces the history of brain-technology hybrid ideas from James Tilly Matthews' 1797 'air loom' delusion to modern tech, arguing cyborg notions run through the industrial age in both fiction and invention.

themes.theme: Origins of mind-control and cyborg ideas

insights.claim: In 1797 James Tilly Matthews was committed to London's Bedlam hospital, convinced a machine he called the 'air loom' controlled his mind via a magnet secretly implanted in his brain.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Early example of machine-control anxieties that recur with each new technology.

insights.claim: Matthews' delusion echoed real cutting-edge technologies in development in the 1980s, two centuries later, which led Mike Jay to trace the history of brain-technology hybrid ideas.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Fears and aspirations around brain-tech long precede the tech, relevant to neurotech narratives.
insights.locator: Jay was fascinated by the echoes

insights.claim: Cyborg notions persisted throughout the industrial age, embedded in science fiction and repeatedly brought to life in scientific invention, though the quest was always incomplete.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Neurotech hype cycles have a long history of unfulfilled promise; calibrate expectations.
